title: Differential-Integral Neural Operator for Long-Term Turbulence Forecasting

problem.claim: Long-term turbulence evolution is difficult to forecast accurately, despite its importance for scientific and engineering applications.

gap.claim: Existing neural operators accumulate errors during long-term autoregressive prediction and fail to preserve physical fidelity because they do not jointly model local dissipative effects and global non-local interactions.

contributions.claim: DINO decomposes turbulent evolution into parallel local differential and global integral operator branches.
The local branch uses a constrained convolutional network designed to converge to a derivative, while the global branch uses a Transformer to learn a data-driven global kernel.
DINO is presented as a physics-based neural operator for stable, robust, long-range turbulence forecasting.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present DINO as a novel framework based on first-principles operator decomposition.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On the 2D Kolmogorov flow benchmark, the authors report a 70% reduction in relative error for 99-step long-term forecasting compared with state-of-the-art models.
The authors report that DINO suppresses error accumulation over hundreds of timesteps and reproduces the theoretical k-3 energy spectrum.
The authors report that code is publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Long-term turbulence forecasting is important but challenging.
Existing neural operators suffer from long-term error accumulation and inadequate physical fidelity.
DINO addresses the gap through explicit differential-integral operator decomposition.
Experiments on 2D Kolmogorov flow are reported to show lower long-term error, reduced accumulation, and spectral fidelity.
The authors characterize DINO as a benchmark for physically consistent long-range forecasting.

source_observation.claim: The method separates local dissipative effects from global non-local interactions using distinct operator branches.

interpretation.claim: Matching model components to distinct structural regimes may improve long-horizon stability.

application.claim: For dynamical forecasting tasks with mixed local and global dependencies, consider explicitly decomposing the learned dynamics into specialized components.

exception.claim: The abstract provides evidence only for the 2D Kolmogorov flow benchmark, so transfer to other dynamical systems is unknown.

unknowns: Training data, evaluation protocol, and baseline identities are unspecified.
The scope of the reported theoretical convergence and stability properties is unspecified.
